props.title: Hitman

sections.content: Hitman (2007) represents one of the earlier major video game adaptations, following Agent 47's chrome-domed assassin into a convoluted plot that largely misses what made the games special. While Timothy Olyphant brings physical presence, the film falls into the same traps as Doom (2005) and BloodRayne (2005) - prioritizing action spectacle over the strategic gameplay elements that defined its source material. The stealth and disguise mechanics that made the Hitman games unique get reduced to generic shoot-outs and car chases.

sections.content: The professional assassin genre found much stronger footing with films like John Wick (2014), which understood that audiences want to see the methodical precision of a master craftsman at work. Collateral (2004) used its hitman premise to explore moral complexity, while Killer Elite (2011) and The Mechanic (2011) leaned into the tradecraft aspects of contract killing. These films succeed by treating assassination as a skill requiring patience and planning rather than just gunplay.

Video game adaptations finally started getting it right with films like Detective Pikachu (2019) and Sonic the Hedgehog (2020), which captured their source material's spirit while working as standalone entertainment. The Hitman reboot Hitman: Agent 47 (2015) made similar mistakes to its predecessor, suggesting that perhaps the methodical stealth gameplay that defines the series remains difficult to translate to film. movies.title: The Bourne Identity
movies.slug: An amnesiac assassin tries to uncover his true identity while evading government agents

sections.content: The modern hitman film owes much to La Femme Nikita (1990) and its American remake Point of No Return (1993), which established many of the genre's conventions. These films portrayed assassination as a profession requiring both physical prowess and psychological complexity. This approach influenced everything from Ghost Dog: The Way of the Samurai (1999) to In Bruges (2008), where the hitman's profession becomes a lens for exploring deeper themes of morality, duty, and redemption.
